title: Morocco Hotel Market H1 2026: Resilience Amid Regional Growth
author: Kōdō Editorial
excerpt: Morocco's hotel sector enters H1 2026 on strong footing, with RevPAR growth across all major destinations driven by record international arrivals and a maturing luxury segment.
content:
Morocco's branded hotel market is delivering its strongest half-year performance on record, with Kōdō data showing national RevPAR reaching MAD 794 across the universe of tracked properties — a 10.8% improvement on the H1 2025 equivalent and a 34% premium over the pre-pandemic baseline of 2019.

Demand Drivers

Three structural forces are converging to underpin the resilience. First, Morocco's Aviation 2030 programme has added over 4 million seats of international capacity since January 2025, with Royal Air Maroc and Ryanair leading new route development into Casablanca, Marrakech and Agadir. Second, the Gulf leisure market — historically a winter-biased segment — has meaningfully extended its booking window into spring and early summer, a pattern confirmed by Kōdō's rate intelligence data showing Gulf-origin bookings running 28% above 2025 levels in the April–June window. Third, the 2026 FIFA World Cup co-hosting effect is already detectable in advance bookings, with Casablanca properties reporting uncommitted group blocks 18 months out.

At MAD 794 national RevPAR, Morocco is now generating higher returns per available room than comparable North African destinations, with a material premium over Tunisia (MAD ~480) and Egypt's Red Sea resort corridor (MAD ~560).

Performance by Segment

The Luxury segment is the standout performer, with occupancy averaging 71.2% and ADR reaching MAD 3,940 — the first time the segment has broken the MAD 3,900 barrier. Ultra Luxury, a small but symbolically important cohort led by Royal Mansour Marrakech and the Four Seasons properties, continues to operate in a demand environment entirely disconnected from macro volatility, with RevPAR exceeding MAD 5,200 on average.

The Upscale segment — Morocco's largest by key count — is posting the most meaningful absolute RevPAR gains, as a cohort of recently repositioned properties in Casablanca and Agadir drives rate compression upward. The Midscale segment, however, is facing margin pressure: energy and labour cost inflation is eroding GOP margins even as occupancy holds above 60%.

City Divergence

Marrakech remains the luxury leader, but Casablanca is closing the gap on an ADR basis, driven by corporate demand growth anchored in the Casa Finance City district. Agadir is the quiet outperformer of H1 2026: resort-format hotels in the Taghazout corridor are running full, with RevPAR up 18% year-on-year. Tanger and Tamuda Bay are benefiting from an emerging Spanish and French weekend leisure market that had not been a meaningful demand source pre-2024.

Kōdō's base case for H2 2026 is continued occupancy growth in the Luxury and Upper Upscale segments, with rate growth moderating as new supply enters the market. The pipeline of 28 confirmed projects representing over 3,800 keys will begin pressuring markets selectively from 2027 — but for now, demand is absorbing capacity with room to spare.

title: The Luxury Pipeline: 5 Hotels That Will Reshape Morocco's Upper Segment by 2028
author: Kōdō Editorial
excerpt: From the Ritz Carlton Tamuda Bay to the Waldorf Astoria Marrakech, Morocco's luxury pipeline represents over MAD 3.5 billion in committed investment — and a fundamental reshaping of the upper-segment competitive landscape.
content:
Morocco's hotel development pipeline is entering a new phase. After a decade dominated by Accor-brand midscale extensions and independent boutique conversions, the country's 2026–2028 confirmed development roster is almost exclusively upper segment — a composition reflecting both the success of Morocco's luxury positioning and the appetite of international operators for a market with demonstrably improving RevPAR fundamentals.

The Five Defining Projects

1. Ritz Carlton Tamuda Bay (2026, 97 keys) — Under construction on the Mediterranean coast in the Tétouan province, this is the most advanced of the five flagship projects. The Ritz Carlton brand's first Morocco entry represents an MAD 920 million investment and will serve the emerging Tamuda Bay resort corridor that has gained significant traction with Spanish and French leisure travellers since 2022. At a projected rack rate of MAD 5,800 per night, it will become the highest-rated hotel asset on Morocco's northern coast.

2. Waldorf Astoria Marrakech (2028, 120 keys) — Hilton's ultra-luxury brand enters Marrakech in a long-anticipated move. With an investment of MAD 1.4 billion, the Waldorf Astoria will compete directly with Royal Mansour and Four Seasons for the top tier of the Marrakech leisure market. The site, in the Palmeraie district, is expected to include 60 garden villas.

The arrival of Waldorf Astoria and Ritz Carlton in Morocco marks the completion of the 'global ultra-luxury brand roster' — every significant tier-1 brand will now have a presence in the kingdom.

3. Ritz Carlton Marrakech (2028, 130 keys) — A second Marriott luxury flagship, complementing the Tamuda Bay property. The Marrakech Ritz Carlton site in the Agdal district is adjacent to the new Mohammed VI Grand Theatre, a positioning that will support cultural tourism demand. Investment: MAD 1.1 billion.

4. Mama Shelter Casablanca (2026, 95 keys) — Accor's lifestyle brand brings a different kind of disruption: not luxury, but design-led urban hospitality aimed at the millennial and Gen-Z professional segment. Casablanca lacks competitive supply in this tier, and Mama Shelter's track record in Paris and Beirut suggests strong opening demand from the corporate and weekend-break market.

5. Fairmont Tanger (2027, 110 keys) — AccorHotels' luxury brand enters Morocco's northern capital in a development that will anchor the regeneration of Tanger's seafront. The Fairmont positioning — experiential luxury at scale — fills a gap in Tanger's offer, which currently lacks a global luxury brand standard property despite strong demand growth.

Market Implications

The aggregate investment in these five properties alone exceeds MAD 3.5 billion. When new supply enters at this quality and price point, it tends to pull the average ADR of the broader luxury segment upward — a dynamic already visible in Dubai post-2019 and Riyadh post-2022. Morocco's branded luxury segment should expect continued ADR growth through 2028, with occupancy stabilising as supply and demand reach a new equilibrium.

title: Casablanca vs Marrakech: A Tale of Two Hotel Markets
author: Kōdō Editorial
excerpt: Morocco's two largest hotel markets serve fundamentally different demand profiles — yet both are outperforming pre-pandemic baselines and generating RevPAR growth that is attracting global operator attention.
content:
Casablanca and Marrakech account for over 60% of Morocco's branded hotel room supply and an even higher share of sector revenues. Yet a comparison of their performance data reveals two hotel markets that are almost mirror images of each other — divergent in demand composition, seasonal profile, and pricing architecture, yet converging in their capacity to generate above-benchmark returns.

Demand Composition

Casablanca is fundamentally a corporate city. Kōdō data shows that approximately 68% of room nights in branded Casablanca hotels are generated by corporate accounts — multinationals, financial institutions, government agencies, and the professional services firms that have clustered around Casa Finance City. This anchors midweek occupancy consistently above 72% even in the shoulder months of November and February, when other Moroccan markets soften. The corollary is that Casablanca is exposed to global corporate travel cycles: a slowdown in financial services activity in the Gulf or Europe would be felt first here.

Marrakech's demand is structurally different. Leisure and MICE (meetings, incentives, conferences, events) account for over 75% of room nights. The city benefits from a 'bucket list' status that sustains both repeat and first-visit leisure demand across European source markets, with Gulf leisure as a fast-growing incremental layer. MICE events — international conferences, incentive groups, destination weddings — fill the luxury and upper upscale hotels at premium ADR rates, particularly in October–November and March–April.

Marrakech generates higher RevPAR than Casablanca on an annual basis — but Casablanca's RevPAR is more stable and less sensitive to seasonal weather events and political news cycles.

Pricing Architecture

Marrakech's luxury segment commands ADR premiums of 35–45% over comparable Casablanca properties, reflecting the resort-luxury positioning and the concentration of ultra-luxury supply (Royal Mansour, Amanjena, Four Seasons Marrakech). Casablanca, by contrast, has a thicker midscale and upscale layer — properties that serve the business traveller market at price points that are competitive with European business hotel benchmarks.

The Convergence Trade

What is changing is Casablanca's luxury ambition. The opening of Four Seasons Casablanca in 2015, followed by the Hyatt Regency repositioning in 2023 and the announced Fairmont Tanger pipeline, signals a market rethinking its tier ceiling. If the upper segment in Casablanca reaches critical mass — four or five properties competing at the MAD 3,500+ ADR level — the city could establish a genuine luxury destination profile rather than solely a business travel hub.

For investors and operators, the strategic choice between the two cities reflects an underlying risk preference. Casablanca offers stable, lower-volatility cash flows anchored by corporate demand. Marrakech offers higher peak RevPAR but greater seasonal exposure. Both are, in Kōdō's view, undervalued relative to comparable North African and Southern Mediterranean markets — and both are positioned to benefit from the structural tailwinds of Morocco's 2030 tourism strategy.
